module_title: Facilities and Equipment for Dairy Farms

lessons.title: Housing systems: freestall, tie-stall, and pasture-based
lessons.body:
Choosing a housing system for your dairy cows depends on your climate, land, and budget. In Africa, three common systems are freestall, tie-stall, and pasture-based. Each has trade-offs in cost, cow comfort, and labour.

Freestall housing gives each cow a clean, dry lying area but allows her to move freely. A typical freestall is 1.2 m wide and 2.4 m long, with a curb to keep bedding in. You need 1 stall per cow. Alleyways behind the stalls should be 2.4â3 m wide for scraping. This system works well in hot climates if you add fans and misters. It costs more to build but reduces bedding use and keeps cows cleaner.

Tie-stall housing ties cows in individual stalls. Each stall is about 1.2 m wide and 1.8 m long. You need a neck rail and a manger. This system uses less space and is cheaper to build, but cows get less exercise and are more prone to lameness. It suits small farms with limited land, but you must clean stalls twice daily and provide daily exercise.

Pasture-based housing lets cows graze on grass. You need a rotational grazing plan with paddocks, a water trough in each paddock, and shade. In Africa, this is the cheapest system, but milk yield depends on grass quality. During dry seasons, you must supplement with hay or silage. A simple shade structure of 3â4 mÂ² per cow is essential. Pasture-based systems need less labour but more landâabout 0.4â0.8 hectares per cow in good rainfall areas.

Many African farms combine systems: cows graze by day and are housed in freestalls at night. Choose based on your resources. If you have land, pasture is cheapest. If you have little land but can invest, freestall is best for cow comfort. Tie-stall is a low-cost option for a few cows, but it demands more daily labour. Always prioritise dry bedding, good ventilation, and easy access to feed and water.

lessons.title: Designing comfortable and efficient barns
lessons.body:
A well-designed barn keeps cows cool, dry, and productive. Start with the site: build on high ground with good drainage, away from swamps and prevailing winds that carry odours. Orient the barn east-west to minimise direct sun on the long sides. In hot African climates, open-sided barns with high roofs (4â5 m at the ridge) allow hot air to rise and escape.

Space per cow is critical. For freestall barns, allow 8â10 mÂ² per cow including alleys. The feed alley should be 3.5â4 m wide for a tractor or feed cart. Water troughs need 60â80 cm of linear space per 10 cows. Place them in alleys, not in stalls, and keep them clean. A cow drinks 60â120 litres per day, so troughs must refill quickly.

Flooring: concrete is best for alleys because it's easy to scrape, but it's hard on hooves. Add grooves every 10 cm for traction. In stalls, use a 10 cm layer of sand, sawdust, or chopped straw. Rubber mats can reduce injuries but are expensive. Slopes: alleys should slope 1â2% toward a drain. Stalls should slope 2% toward the rear so urine drains away.

Ventilation is not optional. Without airflow, cows suffer heat stress and respiratory disease. In open barns, the roof overhang should be at least 1 m. Add ridge vents or cupolas. For closed barns, install fans every 8â10 m along the feed alley. A simple rule: if you can't feel a breeze on your face inside the barn, cows can't either.

Lighting: cows need 16 hours of light per day for milk production. Use LED bulbs or skylights. Provide 200 lux at cow level. Also, design a holding pen near the milking parlourâit should hold 1.5 mÂ² per cow and have a sprinkler system for cooling. Keep the parlour clean and well-lit.

Finally, plan for expansion. Build a barn that can be extended. Use local materials like treated poles, clay bricks, or galvanised iron sheets. A simple, well-ventilated barn with good drainage will outperform an expensive, poorly designed one.

lessons.title: Manure management systems
lessons.body:
A dairy cow produces 15â20 tonnes of manure per year. If not managed, it causes flies, odours, and water pollution. But manure is also a valuable resourceâit can fertilise crops, produce biogas, or be sold. Choose a system that fits your farm and climate.

Solid manure systems: In freestall or tie-stall barns, you scrape manure daily. Use a tractor with a scraper blade or a manual scraper. Push manure to a concrete storage pad. The pad should be 30 cm thick, with a 1% slope to a liquid collection pit. Store solid manure in a heap 1.5â2 m high. Turn it every two weeks to compost. Compost heats to 55â65Â°C, killing weed seeds and pathogens. After 2â3 months, it's ready to apply to fields.

Liquid manure systems: If you use flush water or have a slurry pit, you need a liquid storage tank. A covered tank prevents rain from diluting the slurry and reduces odours. Agitate before pumping. Use a slurry tanker or a hose reel to apply to fields. In Africa, many farms use a simple anaerobic digester to produce biogas for cooking and lighting. A fixed-dome digester for 10 cows costs about $1,500â$3,000 and produces 2â3 mÂ³ of gas per dayâenough for a family.

Daily routine: Scrape alleys twice a day. Remove wet bedding from stalls daily. Add fresh bedding. Keep the manure pad away from wells and streamsâat least 30 m. Flies breed in wet manure, so keep it dry. Use fly traps or parasitic wasps. For odour control, add lime or zeolite to the manure.

If you have limited land, consider selling manure to neighbouring crop farmers. A tonne of composted dairy manure can sell for $20â$50. That turns a waste problem into income. Never dump manure into riversâit kills fish and causes disease. A well-managed manure system keeps your farm clean, reduces disease, and improves soil fertility.

lessons.title: Feed storage and handling equipment
lessons.body:
Feed is the biggest cost in dairy farmingâup to 60% of production. Proper storage prevents spoilage, mould, and nutrient loss. You need three types of storage: for concentrates, for dry roughages (hay), and for silage.

Concentrates: Store in a dry, rodent-proof room. Use metal or plastic bins with tight lids. A 50 kg bag of dairy meal should be used within 4 weeks. Keep bags on pallets, 10 cm off the floor, and away from walls. Label each bin with the date of purchase. Never mix old and new feed. A simple feed bin made from a 200-litre drum with a lid works well. For larger farms, a bulk bin holds 1â2 tonnes and has an auger for dispensing.

Hay: Store in a dry, ventilated shed. Hay must be below 15% moisture before baling, or it will mould and catch fire. Stack bales on a pallet, leaving 30 cm between stacks and walls for air. A shed with a raised floor and open sides is ideal. In humid areas, add a roof vent. Hay stored properly can last 6â12 months. Check for heatingâif the stack is warm, spread it out to dry.

Silage: This is fermented green forage. You need a siloâa pit, bunker, or plastic tube. A bunker silo is cheapest: dig a trench 2 m deep, line with concrete or plastic, and pack chopped maize or grass. Cover with a plastic sheet and weigh it down with tyres. Anaerobic fermentation preserves the feed. After 3â4 weeks, it's ready. Feed out 10â15 cm per day from the face to prevent spoilage. A tube silo (plastic bag) works for small farmsâ50 tonnes capacity for about $300.

Handling equipment: You need a feed cart or wheelbarrow, a shovel, a feed scoop, and a scale. Weigh feed to avoid over- or under-feeding. A simple hanging scale costs $20. For silage, use a silage fork. For concentrates, a bucket. Keep equipment cleanâmouldy feed left in a bucket contaminates fresh feed. Always store feed in a cool, dry place. Protect from rain and sun. Good storage saves money and keeps cows healthy.

lessons.title: Water systems and supply
lessons.body:
Water is the most important nutrient for dairy cows. A lactating cow drinks 60â120 litres per dayâmore in hot weather. She needs water available at all times. If she drinks less, milk yield drops immediately. Your water system must deliver clean, cool water to every cow, every day.

Sources: Boreholes, wells, rivers, dams, and municipal supply. Test water quality annually for bacteria, nitrates, and salts. Clean water has no odour and no visible particles. If using river water, filter and chlorinate. A simple sand filter removes sediment. For bacteria, add 2â5 mg of chlorine per litre. Let it sit for 30 minutes before use.

Storage: You need a tank that holds at least 2 days of water. For 20 cows, that's 4,000 litres. Use a black polyethylene tank to prevent algae growth. Place it on a raised platform 2 m high for gravity flow. Insulate or shade the tankâwater above 25Â°C reduces intake. A concrete tank is cheaper but must be covered.

Distribution: Use PVC pipes (25â40 mm diameter) buried 30 cm deep to prevent damage and keep water cool. Each water trough should be 60â80 cm long per 10 cows. Troughs must be easy to cleanâuse a drain plug. Place troughs in the barn alley and in each paddock. For pasture, use portable troughs connected to a hose. Check troughs twice daily for dirt, algae, and leaks. Clean with a brush and chlorine solution weekly.

Flow rate: A cow can drink 10â20 litres per minute. So a trough valve must deliver at least 10 litres per minute. Use a float valve to maintain level. If pressure is low, install a pressure pump. In hot climates, add a shade over the trough to keep water cool. Also, consider a water meter to track usageâsudden increases may indicate a leak.

Backup: Always have a backup source. A hand pump or a reserve tank can save you if the main supply fails. During dry seasons, water scarcity is common. Harvest rainwater from roofs into tanks. A 100 mÂ² roof collects 1,000 litres from 10 mm of rain. Store it. Water is lifeâfor your cows and your farm.

lessons.title: Ventilation and cooling systems
lessons.body:
Heat stress costs African dairy farmers millions in lost milk. When temperature rises above 25Â°C, cows eat less and produce less. At 35Â°C, milk yield can drop by 20â30%. Ventilation and cooling are not luxuriesâthey are essential.

Natural ventilation: In open barns, use the stack effect. Hot air rises and exits through a ridge vent or open ridge. Cool air enters through open sides. The roof should be 4â5 m high at the ridge, with a 1 m overhang. The building should be at least 15 m wide for good cross-ventilation. Remove any obstructions like hay bales or walls. In tie-stall barns, open the windows and doors. A simple test: hold a ribbon at cow level. If it hangs still, you need more ventilation.

Mechanical ventilation: For closed barns, install fans. Use 1.2 m diameter fans every 8â10 m along the feed alley, angled 15Â° downward. Each fan moves 20,000â30,000 mÂ³/hour. Run them when temperature exceeds 25Â°C. Use a thermostat to control. Fans cost $150â$300 each. Solar-powered fans are available for remote farmsâthey cost more but save on electricity.

Cooling systems: Sprinklers and misters. Sprinklers wet the cow's back and head; as water evaporates, it cools her. Use large droplets (not mist) to soak the skin. Run sprinklers for 2 minutes every 15 minutes when temperature is above 28Â°C. Misters produce fine droplets that cool the air, but they can cause wet bedding and respiratory problems. Use misters only in open, well-ventilated areas. Combine fans with sprinklers for best resultsâthe fan blows air over the wet cow, increasing evaporation.

Shade: In pasture, provide shade trees or shade cloth. A shade structure should provide 3â4 mÂ² per cow. Orient it east-west to block midday sun. White or reflective roofs reflect heat. In the holding pen, install a sprinkler system and fans. Cows wait there before milkingâcool them down.

Water: Ensure cool drinking water. Cows drink more when water is below 20Â°C. Add ice to troughs in extreme heat? Not practical, but shade the trough. Monitor cows for panting, drooling, and reduced feed intakeâthese are signs of heat stress. Act early. A comfortable cow gives more milk.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Facilities and Equipment for Dairy Farms

This practical reference consolidates the core technical and business decisions covered in this module. It is written for African dairy enterprisesâfrom two-cow zero-grazing units to 200-cow commercial herdsâwhere every shilling spent on infrastructure must translate into milk yield, animal health, and labour efficiency. Use it alongside the six lessons as a field guide, a procurement checklist, and a design brief for your contractor or artisan.

1. Housing Systems: Choosing What Fits Your Business Model

Housing is the single largest capital item on a dairy farm after land and cattle. The right system depends on climate, land size, labour availability, and your production target. In Africa, the dominant systems are:

  • Freestall: Cows rest in individual cubicles, with alleyways for walking and feeding. Best for 30+ cows in high-rainfall or high-heat areas. Requires investment in cubicle design, bedding, and alley scraping equipment. Labour-efficient and scalable.
  • Tie-stall: Cows are tethered in individual stalls. Common in Kenya's highlands and parts of Ethiopia. Low initial cost, but high labour demand, poor cow comfort, and difficult mechanisation. Suited to small herds (under 20 cows) with family labour.
  • Pasture-based (including zero-grazing): Cows graze or are cut-and-carried. Zero-grazing units keep cows in a confined area with cut fodder. Low housing cost, but requires reliable forage production and careful manure management. Ideal for mixed crop-livestock farms.

Business-first rule: Choose the system that minimises your cost per litre of milk produced over 10 years, not the one with the lowest upfront cost. A poorly designed tie-stall that costs $200 per cow but reduces yield by 15% will cost more than a $1,000 per cow freestall over a decade.

2. Designing Comfortable and Efficient Barns

Cow comfort is not a luxuryâit is a direct driver of milk yield. Every hour a cow spends standing instead of lying down reduces milk production by approximately 0.5â1 litre per day. The following dimensions are practical minimums for African conditions:

Table 1: Recommended barn dimensions for dairy cattle (adapted for tropical and sub-tropical Africa)
Parameter Small breed (e.g. Jersey, 350â450 kg) Medium breed (e.g. Ayrshire, 450â550 kg) Large breed (e.g. Friesian, 550â650 kg)
Cubicle width 1.10 m 1.20 m 1.25 m
Cubicle length 2.20 m 2.40 m 2.60 m
Feed alley width 3.5 m 3.8 m 4.0 m
Manure alley width 2.5 m 3.0 m 3.2 m
Headroom at ridge 4.5 m 5.0 m 5.5 m
Water trough space per cow 60 cm 70 cm 80 cm
Feed space per cow 60 cm 70 cm 75 cm

Source: FAO (2013), Design and Construction of Dairy Facilities; Kenya Dairy Board (2020), Dairy Farm Infrastructure Guidelines.

Key design principles for African farms:

  • Orientation: East-west ridge line to minimise direct solar gain on the long axis. In hot climates, orient the open side to prevailing winds.
  • Flooring: Grooved concrete with a 1â2% slope to manure alleys. Avoid smooth concreteâit causes slipping and injuries.
  • Roofing: Use reflective or light-coloured roofing (aluminium, galvanised iron painted white) to reduce radiant heat. Insulate if possible.
  • Modularity: Design in modules of 10â20 cows so you can expand without rebuilding. A 20-cow module is the practical minimum for mechanisation.

3. Manure Management Systems

Manure is both a waste and a resource. In Africa, where synthetic fertiliser costs $400â$800 per tonne, manure is worth $15â$30 per tonne as a soil amendment. The system you choose must balance labour, capital, and environmental compliance.

Table 2: Comparison of manure management systems for African dairy farms
System Capital cost (USD/cow) Labour (min/cow/day) Water use Best for
Manual scraping to heap 50â100 8â12 Low Small herds, zero-grazing, dry climates
Slurry (scraper + lagoon) 200â400 4â6 High Medium herds, high-rainfall areas
Biogas digester 300â600 3â5 Medium Farms with 10+ cows, energy needs
Composting (windrow) 80â150 6â10 Low All sizes, organic fertiliser production
Mechanical separator 500â900 2â4 Medium Large herds, bedding recovery

Source: FAO (2018), Manure Management for Smallholder Dairy Farms; ILRI (2019), Waste to Worth: Manure Management in East Africa.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Manure gas and slurry pit hazards

Manure storage pits and lagoons produce hydrogen sulphide (HâS), methane (CHâ), and ammonia (NHâ). HâS is lethal at concentrations above 500 ppm and can cause immediate unconsciousness. Never enter a slurry pit or enclosed manure storage area without a self-contained breathing apparatus and a trained observer. In African farm settings, where confined spaces are common and safety equipment is scarce, the safest rule is: never enterâagitate and pump from outside. Ensure all manure storage areas are fenced and signed. Train all workers on gas hazards during induction and annually thereafter.

4. Feed Storage and Handling Equipment

Feed costs represent 60â70% of milk production costs in Africa. Poor storage causes 10â30% losses to mould, rodents, and insects. Essential equipment includes:

  • Silage bunkers or pits: Concrete or earth-lined, with 2â3 m walls. Capacity: 1.5â2.0 mÂ³ per cow per month for maize silage.
  • Hay barns: Raised floor (30 cm above ground), ventilated walls, roof overhang of at least 1 m. Store bales at 15â18% moisture.
  • Concentrate feed bins: Metal or plastic, rodent-proof, with tight lids. Capacity: 7â10 days of feed per cow.
  • Feed mixer wagon or manual mixing: For herds over 30 cows, a mixer wagon (tractor-drawn or stationary) ensures consistent TMR. For smaller herds, a concrete mixing pad and shovel suffice.
  • Fodder chopper: Motorised or manual. Chopping reduces wastage by 20â30% and improves digestibility.

Business tip: Buy feed storage capacity for 3 months of concentrate and 6 months of forage. This lets you buy at harvest-time low prices and protects against supply disruptions.

5. Water Systems and Supply

A lactating cow drinks 60â120 litres of water per day, depending on yield and temperature. Water is the cheapest feed ingredient and the most neglected. A cow deprived of water for 4 hours can lose 5â10 litres of milk.

  • Source: Borehole, river, rainwater harvesting, or municipal supply. Always have a backup source.
  • Storage: Minimum 3 days of storage for the whole herd. A 10,000-litre tank for 20 cows is a practical minimum.
  • Distribution: Gravity-fed where possible (reduces pumping costs). Use 25â32 mm HDPE pipes for mains, 20 mm for trough lines.
  • Troughs: One trough per 15â20 cows, with a float valve. Clean dailyâalgae and manure reduce intake.
  • Quality: Test water for salinity, nitrates, and bacterial contamination annually. In coastal areas, check for salt intrusion.

6. Ventilation and Cooling Systems

Heat stress costs African dairy farmers millions of litres of milk annually. When the temperature-humidity index (THI) exceeds 72, cows begin to reduce feed intake and milk yield. At THI above 80, yield drops by 10â25%.

  • Natural ventilation: Open ridge (10â15% of floor area), open sidewalls, and 4.5â5.5 m ridge height. This is the cheapest and most reliable system in most of Africa.
  • Fans: Horizontal circulation fans (900â1,200 mm diameter) placed every 10â12 m along the feed alley. Cost: $150â$300 per fan. Running cost: $0.50â$1.00 per day per fan.
  • Sprinklers: Low-pressure sprinklers over the feed alley or holding area. Use 1â2 litres per cow per cycle, 5â10 cycles per day. Combine with fans for evaporative cooling.
  • Shade: In pasture-based systems, provide 3â5 mÂ² of shade per cow. Trees (e.g. Faidherbia albida, Grevillea robusta) are the cheapest option.

Business case: A 20-cow farm in Uganda investing $2,000 in fans and sprinklers can recover the cost in 6â12 months through prevented milk losses during the hot season.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Housing system matches your business model: Freestall for 30+ cows, tie-stall for under 20, pasture/zero-grazing for mixed farms.
  2. Cubicle dimensions are correct for your breed: Width 1.10â1.25 m, length 2.20â2.60 m, with a 1â2% floor slope.
  3. Ventilation is adequate: Open ridge (10â15% of floor area), ridge height 4.5â5.5 m, and cross-ventilation from prevailing winds.
  4. Water supply is reliable: 3 days of storage, one trough per 15â20 cows, and a backup source.
  5. Manure system is planned: Composting or biogas for small herds, slurry or separator for large herds. Never enter a pit.
  6. Feed storage prevents losses: 3 months concentrate, 6 months forage, rodent-proof and moisture-controlled.
  7. Heat stress measures are in place: Shade, fans, or sprinklers when THI exceeds 72.
  8. Safety and training are documented: Gas hazard training, confined space rules, and annual refreshers for all workers.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2013). Design and Construction of Dairy Facilities. Comprehensive technical manual covering housing, ventilation, and waste management.
  • FAO (2018). Manure Management for Smallholder Dairy Farms. Practical guide to composting, biogas, and slurry systems in tropical conditions.
  • ILRI (2019). Waste to Worth: Manure Management in East Africa. Case studies and economic analysis from Kenyan and Ethiopian dairy farms.
  • Kenya Dairy Board (2020). Dairy Farm Infrastructure Guidelines. Localised standards for barn design, water systems, and manure handling in East Africa.
  • FAO Dairy Production and Products Portal. Free access to technical guides, case studies, and training materials for African dairy development.

This practical reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Dairy Production, module Facilities and Equipment for Dairy Farms. Use it as a field checklist and a basis for your farm infrastructure investment plan.

quiz.q: What is the recommended width of a freestall for a dairy cow?
quiz.explanation: A freestall should be 1.2 m wide to allow the cow to lie comfortably.

quiz.q: Which housing system ties cows in individual stalls?
quiz.explanation: Tie-stall housing ties cows in place, limiting movement.

quiz.q: In pasture-based systems, how much land per cow is needed in good rainfall areas?
quiz.explanation: 0.4â0.8 hectares per cow is typical for grazing in good rainfall areas.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of freestall housing?
options: C) Cleaner cows and less bedding use
quiz.explanation: Freestalls keep cows cleaner and reduce bedding use compared to tie-stalls.

quiz.q: Which system is cheapest to build but requires more daily labour?
quiz.explanation: Tie-stall is low-cost but demands twice-daily cleaning and exercise.

quiz.q: What is the ideal orientation for a dairy barn in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: East-west orientation minimises direct sun on the long sides of the barn.

quiz.q: How much space per cow should be allowed in a freestall barn including alleys?
quiz.explanation: 8â10 mÂ² per cow provides adequate space for movement and feeding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended slope for alleys in a dairy barn?
quiz.explanation: A 1â2% slope allows proper drainage without being slippery.

quiz.q: How much linear water trough space is needed per 10 cows?
quiz.explanation: 60â80 cm of trough space per 10 cows ensures adequate access.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation critical in dairy barns?
options: B) To reduce heat stress and respiratory disease
quiz.explanation: Good ventilation removes heat and moisture, preventing heat stress and disease.

quiz.q: How much manure does a dairy cow produce per year?
quiz.explanation: A dairy cow produces 15â20 tonnes of manure annually.

quiz.q: What temperature does compost reach to kill pathogens?
quiz.explanation: Compost heats to 55â65Â°C, which kills weed seeds and pathogens.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of a covered liquid manure tank?
options: B) Prevents rain dilution and reduces odours
quiz.explanation: A cover prevents rainwater from diluting slurry and reduces odour release.

quiz.q: How far should a manure pad be from wells and streams?
quiz.explanation: At least 30 m prevents water contamination.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to control flies in manure?
quiz.explanation: Flies breed in wet manure, so keeping it dry reduces breeding.

quiz.q: What is the maximum moisture content for safe hay storage?
quiz.explanation: Hay above 15% moisture can mould and spontaneously combust.

quiz.q: How long should silage ferment before feeding?
quiz.explanation: Silage needs 3â4 weeks of anaerobic fermentation to stabilise.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily feed-out rate from a silage face?
quiz.explanation: Feeding out 10â15 cm per day prevents spoilage and secondary fermentation.

quiz.q: Why should feed bags be kept on pallets?
options: B) To prevent moisture and rodent damage
C) To make them easier to count
D) To allow air circulation only
quiz.explanation: Pallets keep bags off the floor, preventing moisture absorption and rodent access.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective silo for small farms?
quiz.explanation: A plastic tube silo is affordable and effective for small-scale silage storage.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating dairy cow drink per day?
quiz.explanation: A lactating cow drinks 60â120 litres daily, more in hot weather.

quiz.q: What is the minimum water storage capacity for 20 cows for 2 days?
quiz.explanation: 20 cows x 100 litres/day x 2 days = 4,000 litres.

quiz.q: Why should water tanks be shaded or insulated?
options: A) To prevent algae and keep water cool
B) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Shade reduces algae growth and keeps water below 25Â°C, encouraging intake.

quiz.q: What is the recommended flow rate for a water trough valve?
quiz.explanation: Cows can drink 10â20 litres per minute, so valves must deliver at least that.

quiz.q: How much rainwater can a 100 mÂ² roof collect from 10 mm of rain?
quiz.explanation: 100 mÂ² x 0.01 m = 1 mÂ³ = 1,000 litres.

quiz.q: At what temperature does heat stress begin to reduce milk yield?
quiz.explanation: Milk yield starts to drop when temperature exceeds 25Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height of a barn ridge for natural ventilation?
quiz.explanation: A ridge height of 4â5 m allows hot air to rise and escape.

quiz.q: How often should sprinklers run in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: Cycling sprinklers for 2 minutes every 15 minutes cools cows without wasting water.

quiz.q: What is a sign of heat stress in dairy cows?
quiz.explanation: Panting and drooling are classic signs of heat stress.

quiz.q: How much shade space per cow is recommended in pasture?
quiz.explanation: 3â4 mÂ² per cow provides adequate shade to reduce heat load.
